MASTER PROJECT PROMPT — SECURELAUNCH

Act as a senior full-stack engineer, application security engineer, software architect, and UI/UX designer.

Your task is to build a production-minded web application called SecureLaunch.

SecureLaunch is an OWASP-based website security assessment platform that helps developers identify security weaknesses in their websites before publishing them.

Do not just create a frontend design or a demonstration dashboard. Build a functional application with a real backend, database, security scanning integration, background jobs, and a professional interface.

Make good engineering decisions independently. Do not stop to ask me which programming language or framework to use.

1. PROJECT OBJECTIVE

Build a platform where developers can:

  1. Create an account and log in.

  2. Register a website they own or are authorized to test.

  3. Verify ownership of the website.

  4. Start a security assessment against their staging website.

  5. Automatically scan for detectable security weaknesses.

  6. Receive a security assessment based on all 10 OWASP Top 10:2025 categories.

  7. See security ratings and vulnerability counts in a dashboard.

  8. Open individual findings to understand exactly what is wrong.

  9. Receive clear, actionable instructions explaining how to fix each weakness.

  10. Run another scan to verify whether the weakness has been fixed.

The long-term objective is to evolve SecureLaunch into a professional application security testing platform with CI/CD integration, source-code analysis, authenticated scanning, and advanced security reporting.

2. TECHNOLOGY STACK

Use the following technologies.

Frontend:

  • React

  • Next.js with App Router

  • TypeScript

  • Tailwind CSS

  • shadcn/ui for reusable components

  • Recharts for charts

  • Lucide icons

Backend:

  • Next.js server-side APIs

  • TypeScript

  • Zod for input validation

  • Modular service architecture

Database:

  • PostgreSQL

  • Prisma ORM

Background jobs:

  • Redis

  • BullMQ

Security scanning:

  • OWASP ZAP Docker image

  • ZAP Baseline Scan for the initial scanning engine

  • Custom HTTP security configuration checks

  • Architecture that allows future Semgrep and software composition analysis integrations

Infrastructure:

  • Docker

  • Docker Compose for local infrastructure

  • Environment variables for configuration

Use a pnpm monorepo or another clean, maintainable project structure.

Keep the code modular. Do not put all application logic inside one file.

3. OWASP TOP 10:2025 INTEGRATION

The application MUST display all ten categories.

Use the official OWASP Top 10:2025 classification.

A01:2025 — Broken Access Control

Assess:

  • Publicly accessible restricted resources where detectable.

  • Potential access-control weaknesses.

  • Authentication and authorization boundaries when test accounts are configured.

A02:2025 — Security Misconfiguration

Assess:

  • Missing security headers.

  • Insecure HTTP configuration.

  • Incorrect cookie security flags.

  • Directory listing exposure.

  • Information disclosure.

  • Insecure server configuration where detectable.

A03:2025 — Software Supply Chain Failures

Plan checks for:

  • Vulnerable third-party dependencies.

  • Outdated packages.

  • Dependency integrity.

  • Lockfiles and dependency configuration.

  • CI/CD pipeline security.

This category requires repository or dependency information. Do not claim it has passed based only on a website URL.

A04:2025 — Cryptographic Failures

Assess:

  • TLS configuration.

  • Invalid or expired certificates.

  • Insecure transport.

  • Mixed content.

  • Insecure cookie configuration.

  • Other externally detectable cryptographic weaknesses.

Clearly distinguish between externally detectable issues and encryption controls that require source-code or infrastructure access.

A05:2025 — Injection

Assess detectable indicators of:

  • SQL injection.

  • Cross-site scripting.

  • Command injection.

  • Other injection weaknesses.

Use safe scanning by default. Any future active testing must require explicit authorization and a designated staging target.

A06:2025 — Insecure Design

Prepare assessment support for:

  • Threat modeling.

  • Business logic weaknesses.

  • Design-level security requirements.

  • Trust boundaries.

  • Security architecture reviews.

Mark this category REVIEW REQUIRED when automated evidence is insufficient.

A07:2025 — Authentication Failures

Assess:

  • Login and authentication configuration where detectable.

  • Session management.

  • Cookie security.

  • Authentication-related misconfiguration.

  • Weak authentication controls where testable.

Support authenticated security testing in a future module.

A08:2025 — Software or Data Integrity Failures

Assess:

  • Subresource Integrity where applicable.

  • Client-side resource integrity indicators.

  • Dependency integrity.

  • Software update integrity.

  • CI/CD integrity configuration where repository information is available.

A09:2025 — Security Logging and Alerting Failures

Prepare checks for:

  • Security logging configuration.

  • Audit logging.

  • Monitoring configuration.

  • Security event detection.

  • Alerting configuration.

Do not claim that logging and alerting work correctly just because a public website responds successfully.

A10:2025 — Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions

Assess:

  • Detailed error disclosure.

  • Stack traces exposed to users.

  • Unexpected HTTP error behavior.

  • Information leakage through error responses.

  • Observable exception-handling weaknesses.

Source-code and test-based checks should be added later for stronger coverage.

IMPORTANT:

Every OWASP category must always appear in the report, even when it cannot be automatically assessed.

Use these assessment statuses:

  • PASS: All defined checks for that assessment completed without detecting an issue.

  • ISSUES FOUND: One or more weaknesses were detected.

  • REVIEW REQUIRED: Additional human or source-code review is needed.

  • PARTIAL: Some checks were completed, but coverage is incomplete.

  • NOT TESTED: No applicable check was performed.

Never mark a category PASS just because the scanner did not find anything.

4. WEBSITE REGISTRATION AND OWNERSHIP VERIFICATION

Build a website registration system.

A developer should be able to enter a domain such as:

https://example.com

Before scanning, require proof that the user controls the domain or is authorized to test it.

Implement:

  • DNS TXT verification.

  • An alternative HTTP verification file under a well-known path.

  • Verification token generation.

  • Token expiration.

  • Verified/unverified status.

  • Asset ownership checks.

Prevent users from scanning websites they do not control.

Implement strict SSRF protections:

  • Allow only supported HTTP/HTTPS URLs.

  • Block loopback addresses.

  • Block private and internal IP addresses.

  • Block link-local and cloud metadata addresses.

  • Validate IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

  • Check DNS resolution and protect against DNS rebinding.

  • Validate redirects and prevent redirecting outside the authorized scope.

  • Restrict production scanning to verified assets.

  • Do not allow arbitrary ports or unrestricted network destinations.

Local development targets may be supported only through an explicit development-only configuration. Never enable that behavior in production by default.

5. SECURITY SCANNING ENGINE

Integrate OWASP ZAP as the initial real scanning engine.

The first version must use the official ZAP Baseline Scan.

The scan workflow should:

  1. Receive a scan request.

  2. Verify that the asset belongs to the authenticated user.

  3. Confirm the asset is verified.

  4. Validate the target and its network scope again inside the worker.

  5. Add a scan job to BullMQ.

  6. Start an isolated ZAP Docker scan.

  7. Collect the scan output.

  8. Parse the ZAP JSON report.

  9. Map the findings to the appropriate OWASP categories.

  10. Save the results in PostgreSQL.

  11. Update the scan status.

  12. Make the results available in the dashboard.

Implement scan statuses:

  • QUEUED

  • INITIALIZING

  • RUNNING

  • COMPLETED

  • FAILED

  • CANCELLED

Use a scan timeout, request-rate limits, concurrency limits, and page limits.

IMPORTANT SECURITY REQUIREMENTS:

  • Passive scanning must be the default.

  • Do not perform destructive testing.

  • Do not perform denial-of-service testing.

  • Do not brute-force accounts.

  • Do not attempt credential guessing.

  • Do not exfiltrate data.

  • Do not run arbitrary shell commands supplied by users.

  • Do not scan outside the verified target scope.

  • Do not expose the ZAP management API publicly.

  • Isolate scanning infrastructure from the main application.

  • Restrict scanner resource consumption and network access.

Future active scanning must be a separate feature with explicit authorization, staging-environment restrictions, and additional safeguards.

Create a scanner adapter interface so other scanning engines can be integrated without rewriting the application.

6. SECURITY FINDINGS AND REMEDIATION

This is one of the most important parts of the application.

Do not merely show a vulnerability name.

For every finding, store and display:

  • Finding title.

  • OWASP category.

  • Severity.

  • Confidence level.

  • Affected URL.

  • HTTP method when available.

  • Affected parameter when available.

  • Technical description.

  • Evidence supporting the finding.

  • Why the issue matters.

  • Potential impact.

  • Step-by-step remediation instructions.

  • Example of a secure configuration or code pattern where applicable.

  • Links to relevant official security documentation.

  • Detection source.

  • First detected date.

  • Finding status.

Severity levels:

  • CRITICAL

  • HIGH

  • MEDIUM

  • LOW

  • INFORMATIONAL

Allow developers to:

  • Mark findings as open.

  • Mark findings as in progress.

  • Mark findings as fixed.

  • Retest findings with a new scan.

  • Track resolved and recurring weaknesses.

IMPORTANT:

If only a URL was scanned, do not invent source-code file names or line numbers.

For URL-based findings, identify the affected endpoint and provide evidence.

When source-code analysis is added, provide exact file paths and line numbers if the scanner returns them.

Remediation advice must be related to actual evidence, not generic or fabricated claims.

7. SECURITY SCORING SYSTEM

Create a transparent assessment scoring system.

Every OWASP row should display:

  • Category.

  • Assessment status.

  • Risk rating.

  • Number of findings.

  • Highest severity detected.

  • Assessment coverage.

The overall dashboard should display:

  • Total security findings.

  • Critical findings.

  • High findings.

  • Medium findings.

  • Low findings.

  • Resolved findings.

  • Assessment coverage percentage.

  • Overall risk index.

Use an explainable initial risk formula:

Risk deductions:

  • Critical: 20 points.

  • High: 10 points.

  • Medium: 4 points.

  • Low: 1 point.

Overall risk index:

100 minus the total severity deductions, with a minimum of zero.

Show the formula in the UI.

Clearly label this as an internal, provisional risk index, not an official OWASP certification or proof that a website is secure.

Always show scan coverage alongside the score. Incomplete assessments must be clearly marked as provisional.

Do not confuse absence of detected findings with proof of security.

5. One important thing about the future

Don't stop at OWASP Top 10.

The next major evolution should be combining three types of security testing:

DAST — Dynamic Application Security Testing

Tests a running website. OWASP ZAP is our starting point.

SAST — Static Application Security Testing

Examines source code and helps developers find the exact vulnerable files and lines.

SCA — Software Composition Analysis

Identifies vulnerable third-party libraries and dependencies.

Together, these make SecureLaunch much more useful than a simple website vulnerability scanner.

Useful official references:

  • OWASP Top 10:2025

  • OWASP ZAP

  • OWASP Application Security Verification Standard 5.0

  • OWASP Dependency-Check

My advice: First make the registration → verification → real scan → results → fix → retest workflow work perfectly. That is the foundation of your product. Then we can grow it into a full application security platform. 🚀

  10. Run another scan to verify whether the weakness has been fixed.

The long-term objective is to evolve SecureLaunch into a professional application security testing platform with CI/CD integration, source-code analysis, authenticated scanning, and advanced security reporting.

2. TECHNOLOGY STACK

Use the following technologies.

Frontend:

  • React
  • Next.js with App Router
  • TypeScript
  • Tailwind CSS
  • shadcn/ui for reusable components
  • Recharts for charts
  • Lucide icons

Backend:

  • Next.js server-side APIs
  • TypeScript
  • Zod for input validation
  • Modular service architecture

Database:

  • PostgreSQL
  • Prisma ORM

Background jobs:

  • Redis
  • BullMQ

Security scanning:

  • OWASP ZAP Docker image
  • ZAP Baseline Scan for the initial scanning engine
  • Custom HTTP security configuration checks
  • Architecture that allows future Semgrep and software composition analysis integrations

Infrastructure:

  • Docker
  • Docker Compose for local infrastructure
  • Environment variables for configuration

Use a pnpm monorepo or another clean, maintainable project structure.

Keep the code modular. Do not put all application logic inside one file.

3. OWASP TOP 10:2025 INTEGRATION

The application MUST display all ten categories.

Use the official OWASP Top 10:2025 classification.

A01:2025 — Broken Access Control

Assess:

  • Publicly accessible restricted resources where detectable.
  • Potential access-control weaknesses.
  • Authentication and authorization boundaries when test accounts are configured.

A02:2025 — Security Misconfiguration

Assess:

  • Missing security headers.
  • Insecure HTTP configuration.
  • Incorrect cookie security flags.
  • Directory listing exposure.
  • Information disclosure.
  • Insecure server configuration where detectable.

A03:2025 — Software Supply Chain Failures

Plan checks for:

  • Vulnerable third-party dependencies.
  • Outdated packages.
  • Dependency integrity.
  • Lockfiles and dependency configuration.
  • CI/CD pipeline security.

This category requires repository or dependency information. Do not claim it has passed based only on a website URL.

A04:2025 — Cryptographic Failures

Assess:

  • TLS configuration.
  • Invalid or expired certificates.
  • Insecure transport.
  • Mixed content.
  • Insecure cookie configuration.
  • Other externally detectable cryptographic weaknesses.

Clearly distinguish between externally detectable issues and encryption controls that require source-code or infrastructure access.

A05:2025 — Injection

Assess detectable indicators of:

  • SQL injection.
  • Cross-site scripting.
  • Command injection.
  • Other injection weaknesses.

Use safe scanning by default. Any future active testing must require explicit authorization and a designated staging target.

A06:2025 — Insecure Design

Prepare assessment support for:

  • Threat modeling.
  • Business logic weaknesses.
  • Design-level security requirements.
  • Trust boundaries.
  • Security architecture reviews.

Mark this category REVIEW REQUIRED when automated evidence is insufficient.

A07:2025 — Authentication Failures

Assess:

  • Login and authentication configuration where detectable.
  • Session management.
  • Cookie security.
  • Authentication-related misconfiguration.
  • Weak authentication controls where testable.

Support authenticated security testing in a future module.

A08:2025 — Software or Data Integrity Failures

Assess:

  • Subresource Integrity where applicable.
  • Client-side resource integrity indicators.
  • Dependency integrity.
  • Software update integrity.
  • CI/CD integrity configuration where repository information is available.

A09:2025 — Security Logging and Alerting Failures

Prepare checks for:

  • Security logging configuration.
  • Audit logging.
  • Monitoring configuration.
  • Security event detection.
  • Alerting configuration.

Do not claim that logging and alerting work correctly just because a public website responds successfully.

A10:2025 — Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions

Assess:

  • Detailed error disclosure.
  • Stack traces exposed to users.
  • Unexpected HTTP error behavior.
  • Information leakage through error responses.
  • Observable exception-handling weaknesses.

Source-code and test-based checks should be added later for stronger coverage.

IMPORTANT:

Every OWASP category must always appear in the report, even when it cannot be automatically assessed.

Use these assessment statuses:

  • PASS: All defined checks for that assessment completed without detecting an issue.
  • ISSUES FOUND: One or more weaknesses were detected.
  • REVIEW REQUIRED: Additional human or source-code review is needed.
  • PARTIAL: Some checks were completed, but coverage is incomplete.
  • NOT TESTED: No applicable check was performed.

Never mark a category PASS just because the scanner did not find anything.

4. WEBSITE REGISTRATION AND OWNERSHIP VERIFICATION

Build a website registration system.

A developer should be able to enter a domain such as:

https://example.com

Before scanning, require proof that the user controls the domain or is authorized to test it.

Implement:

  • DNS TXT verification.
  • An alternative HTTP verification file under a well-known path.
  • Verification token generation.
  • Token expiration.
  • Verified/unverified status.
  • Asset ownership checks.

Prevent users from scanning websites they do not control.

Implement strict SSRF protections:

  • Allow only supported HTTP/HTTPS URLs.
  • Block loopback addresses.
  • Block private and internal IP addresses.
  • Block link-local and cloud metadata addresses.
  • Validate IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
  • Check DNS resolution and protect against DNS rebinding.
  • Validate redirects and prevent redirecting outside the authorized scope.
  • Restrict production scanning to verified assets.
  • Do not allow arbitrary ports or unrestricted network destinations.

Local development targets may be supported only through an explicit development-only configuration. Never enable that behavior in production by default.

5. SECURITY SCANNING ENGINE

Integrate OWASP ZAP as the initial real scanning engine.

The first version must use the official ZAP Baseline Scan.

The scan workflow should:

  1. Receive a scan request.
  2. Verify that the asset belongs to the authenticated user.
  3. Confirm the asset is verified.
  4. Validate the target and its network scope again inside the worker.
  5. Add a scan job to BullMQ.
  6. Start an isolated ZAP Docker scan.
  7. Collect the scan output.
  8. Parse the ZAP JSON report.
  9. Map the findings to the appropriate OWASP categories.
  10. Save the results in PostgreSQL.
  11. Update the scan status.
  12. Make the results available in the dashboard.

Implement scan statuses:

  • QUEUED
  • INITIALIZING
  • RUNNING
  • COMPLETED
  • FAILED
  • CANCELLED

Use a scan timeout, request-rate limits, concurrency limits, and page limits.

IMPORTANT SECURITY REQUIREMENTS:

  • Passive scanning must be the default.
  • Do not perform destructive testing.
  • Do not perform denial-of-service testing.
  • Do not brute-force accounts.
  • Do not attempt credential guessing.
  • Do not exfiltrate data.
  • Do not run arbitrary shell commands supplied by users.
  • Do not scan outside the verified target scope.
  • Do not expose the ZAP management API publicly.
  • Isolate scanning infrastructure from the main application.
  • Restrict scanner resource consumption and network access.

Future active scanning must be a separate feature with explicit authorization, staging-environment restrictions, and additional safeguards.

Create a scanner adapter interface so other scanning engines can be integrated without rewriting the application.

6. SECURITY FINDINGS AND REMEDIATION

This is one of the most important parts of the application.

Do not merely show a vulnerability name.

For every finding, store and display:

  • Finding title.
  • OWASP category.
  • Severity.
  • Confidence level.
  • Affected URL.
  • HTTP method when available.
  • Affected parameter when available.
  • Technical description.
  • Evidence supporting the finding.
  • Why the issue matters.
  • Potential impact.
  • Step-by-step remediation instructions.
  • Example of a secure configuration or code pattern where applicable.
  • Links to relevant official security documentation.
  • Detection source.
  • First detected date.
  • Finding status.

Severity levels:

  • CRITICAL
  • HIGH
  • MEDIUM
  • LOW
  • INFORMATIONAL

Allow developers to:

  • Mark findings as open.
  • Mark findings as in progress.
  • Mark findings as fixed.
  • Retest findings with a new scan.
  • Track resolved and recurring weaknesses.

IMPORTANT:

If only a URL was scanned, do not invent source-code file names or line numbers.

For URL-based findings, identify the affected endpoint and provide evidence.

When source-code analysis is added, provide exact file paths and line numbers if the scanner returns them.

Remediation advice must be related to actual evidence, not generic or fabricated claims.
